title: ذُو and ذَات with the Dual, the Man of Two Faces, and Lesson 21: لَمْ
summary: Finishing the dual, the class uses ذُو and ذَات to describe things by what they possess — الْقَمِيص ذُو الْجَيْبَيْنِ, the shirt with two pockets — and works out why the description must carry أل when the thing described does. The idiom رَجُل ذُو وَجْهَيْنِ gives a two-faced man, which the lesson then defines in Arabic. Lesson twenty-one opens with لَمْ, the strangest of the negations so far: it attaches to a مُضَارِع verb, makes it sākin, and yet means the past.
key_points: لَمْ attaches to a مُضَارِع verb but carries مَاضِي meaning, and it puts the verb in jazm with a sukūn: لَمْ يَذْهَبْ means he did not go.

With a plural or a dual, لَمْ cannot add a sukūn to an ending already fixed, so it drops the نُون instead — يَذْهَبُونَ becomes لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا and the dual يَذْهَبَانِ becomes لَمْ يَذْهَبَا — exactly as لَنْ does.
The negations now in hand: لَا for the present and future, مَا chiefly for the past, لَنْ for the future with emphasis, and لَمْ for the past using a مُضَارِع form.

لَمْ and مَا mean the same thing — both negate the past. They differ in form, مَا taking the مَاضِي and لَمْ the مُضَارِع made sākin. Which sounds more fitting in a given sentence is a matter of feel acquired from reading, not a rule.
أَحَدُهُمَا … وَالْآخَر is used of two; for three or more it is أَحَدُهُمْ. The dual of أَخ is أَخَوَانِ, as against the plural إِخْوَان.
There is no need to repeat أَحَد for the second item: one says أَحَدُهُمَا طَبِيبٌ وَالْآخَرُ مُهَنْدِسٌ, just as in Urdu or English.
ذُو means the possessor of and ذَات is its feminine, and either can serve as a صِفَة: الْقَمِيص ذُو الْجَيْبَيْنِ، تِلْكَ الْغُرْفَة ذَات النَّافِذَتَيْنِ الْمَفْتُوحَتَيْنِ.

A صِفَة must match its مَوْصُوف in four things, among them definiteness. So where the مَوْصُوف carries أل, the صِفَة must too — hence الْقَمِيص ذُو الْجَيْبَيْنِ with ذُو made definite by its مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ.
The صِفَة agrees with the thing described, not with the thing possessed: ذَلِكَ الْمَسْجِد ذُو الْمَنَارَتَيْنِ جَمِيلٌ is masculine because مَسْجِد is, even though مَنَارَة is feminine.

رَجُل ذُو وَجْهَيْنِ is a man of two faces — the Arabic for a two-faced or hypocritical person, defined in the lesson as الَّذِي يَأْتِي هَؤُلَاءِ بِوَجْهٍ وَهَؤُلَاءِ بِوَجْهٍ, one who comes to each group with whatever pleases them.

أَحْمَدُ اللَّهَ وَأَشْكُرُهُ attributes the praise to the speaker — I praise Allah and thank Him — as against the plain الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ. The plural نَحْمَدُهُ وَنَشْكُرُهُ is what opens a bayān, where all present praise together.
The relative pronouns for the feminine: الَّتِي singular, اللَّتَانِ dual, and اللَّاتِي or اللَّائِي plural.
حَضَرَ، يَحْضُرُ means to be present or to attend, giving حَاضِر.

Vocabulary: حَافِلَة (bus), مُفِيد (beneficial, as in Urdu), سِيرَة (a biography, and particularly the life of the Prophet ﷺ), تَفْسِير (explanation of the Qur'ān) as against تَرْجَمَة (translation), شَرَحَ (to explain), ذَبَحَ (to slaughter), and جَيْب (pocket) with its dual جَيْبَيْنِ.
questions: [00:03:00] Q: Why is it أَحَدُهُمَا and not أَحَدُهُمْ? — A: Because هُمْ is for three or more, while هُمَا is the dual — and here there are only two brothers.
[00:03:00] Q: Do you have to repeat أَحَد for the second one? — A: No; you simply say وَالْآخَر, exactly as you would in Urdu or English.
[00:06:12] Q: Is بَيْضَاء the word for white? — A: Yes, it is the feminine of أَبْيَض. بَيْض, with a different vowel, means eggs.
[00:08:05] Q: Why is it رِسَالَتَيْنِ and not رِسَالَتَانِ? — A: Because it is the object — the thing written — so it takes the ـَيْنِ form.
[00:12:01] Q: Why does ذُو carry أل here? — A: Because a صِفَة must match its مَوْصُوف in definiteness, and الْقَمِيص has أل, so its description must be definite too.
[00:16:06] Q: Shouldn't it be جَمِيلَة, since مَنَارَة is feminine? — A: No. The adjective describes the masjid, not the minaret, and مَسْجِد is masculine.
[00:17:06] Q: Does ذُو وَجْهَيْنِ mean he literally has two faces? — A: No — it is the Arabic idiom for a two-faced person, one who presents a different face to each group.

[00:25:00] Q: Is أَحْمَدُ اللَّهَ different from الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ? — A: Both are correct; the first attributes the praising to yourself — I praise Allah — while the second simply states that all praise belongs to Him.
[00:30:00] Q: Why has the yāʾ dropped in لَمْ يَأْتِ? — A: Because لَمْ makes the verb sākin, and that type of verb loses its final letter in the process — a form covered later.

[00:31:00] Q: Why not just use مَا instead of لَمْ? — A: In meaning they are the same; the difference is formal. Which fits better in a given sentence is something you come to feel from reading a great deal of Arabic.

quiz.q: Which verb form does لَمْ attach to, and which tense does it mean?
options: The مُضَارِع, but meaning the past
quiz.a: لَمْ يَذْهَبْ uses the present-tense form but means he did not go.

quiz.q: What does لَمْ do to a singular verb's ending?
quiz.a: It puts the verb in jazm — لَمْ يَلِدْ, with a sukūn.

quiz.q: What happens when لَمْ meets a plural verb such as يَرَوْنَ?
options: The نُون is dropped, giving لَمْ يَرَوْا
quiz.a: There is no room for a sukūn, so the نُون falls away — as in أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا.

quiz.q: How do لَمْ and مَا differ?
options: لَمْ is for the future, مَا for the past
They mean the same; لَمْ takes the مُضَارِع made sākin, مَا takes the مَاضِي
مَا is emphatic, لَمْ is not
لَمْ can only be used in questions
quiz.a: Both negate the past. The difference is in form, and which one suits a sentence is learned by exposure.

quiz.q: What does ذُو mean, and what is its feminine?
quiz.a: ذُو الْجَيْبَيْنِ for a masculine noun, ذَات النَّافِذَتَيْنِ for a feminine one.

quiz.q: Why must ذُو carry أل when describing الْقَمِيص?
options: Because a صِفَة must match its مَوْصُوف in definiteness
quiz.a: Agreement in definiteness is one of the four things a صِفَة must share with its مَوْصُوف.

quiz.q: In ذَلِكَ الْمَسْجِد ذُو الْمَنَارَتَيْنِ ـــــ, which adjective is correct?
quiz.a: The adjective describes the masjid, which is masculine — not the feminine مَنَارَة.

quiz.q: What does رَجُل ذُو وَجْهَيْنِ mean?
options: A man with a scarred face
A two-faced man — a hypocrite who shows each group a different face
quiz.a: The lesson defines him as الَّذِي يَأْتِي هَؤُلَاءِ بِوَجْهٍ وَهَؤُلَاءِ بِوَجْهٍ.

quiz.q: What is أَحَدُهُمَا used for, as against أَحَدُهُمْ?
options: أَحَدُهُمَا for exactly two; أَحَدُهُمْ for three or more
quiz.a: هُمَا is the dual pronoun, هُمْ the plural.

quiz.q: What is the dual relative pronoun for the feminine?
quiz.a: الَّتِي is singular, اللَّتَانِ dual, and اللَّاتِي or اللَّائِي plural.

quran_examples.translation: He neither begets nor is born.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's first and most familiar example of لَمْ: يَلِدُ from وَلَدَ، يَلِدُ becomes يَلِدْ with the sukūn, while the sense is past — He did not beget.

quran_examples.translation: Did there not come to you a warner?
quran_examples.note: Raised by a student from Sūrat al-Mulk, and the teacher used it to show that a verb of this type loses its final yāʾ when لَمْ makes it sākin — يَأْتِي becoming يَأْتِ.

quran_examples.arabic: أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا إِلَى الطَّيْرِ فَوْقَهُمْ صَافَّاتٍ وَيَقْبِضْنَ
quran_examples.transliteration: a-wa-lam yaraw ilā al-ṭayri fawqahum ṣāffātin wa-yaqbiḍn
quran_examples.translation: Do they not see the birds above them with wings outspread and folded in?
quran_examples.note: The plural case: يَرَوْنَ loses its نُون after لَمْ. صَافَّاتٍ is also a جَمْع مُؤَنَّث سَالِم with its kasra, and يَقْبِضْنَ carries نُون النِّسْوَة.

quran_examples.arabic: لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنفَكِّينَ حَتَّىٰ تَأْتِيَهُمُ الْبَيِّنَةُ
quran_examples.transliteration: lam yakuni alladhīna kafarū min ahli al-kitābi wa-l-mushrikīna munfakkīna ḥattā taʾtiyahumu al-bayyinah
quran_examples.translation: Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to be parted until the clear evidence came to them.
quran_examples.note: Cited in class as a sūrah opening with لَمْ. كَانَ، يَكُونُ becomes يَكُنْ in jazm, and the kasra appears only because the following word begins with a connecting hamza.
